citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing linear in the first argument ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]). Write $H\odot K$ for the complex vector space of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] applied to $R=\mathbb C$ and the $\mathbb C$-modules $H,K$: its underlying abelian group is the quotient $F/H_0$ of that definition, the class of $e_{(u,v)}$ is written $u\otimes v$, every element of $H\odot K$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $u\otimes v$, and the defining relations make $(u,v)\mapsto u\otimes v$ $\mathbb C$-bilinear. Define, for finite sums, $$\Bigl\langle\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i,\ \sum_j u'_j\otimes v'_j\Bigr\rangle:=\sum_{i,j}\langle u_i,u'_j\rangle_H\,\langle v_i,v'_j\rangle_K .$$ Then: (a) *well-definedness and sesquilinearity*: the displayed value is independent of the representatives of its two arguments and defines a Hermitian sesquilinear form on $H\odot K$, linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; (b) *positive definiteness and orthonormal coordinates*: $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ for every $z\in H\odot K$, with $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ exactly for $z=0$; more precisely, if $U_0\subseteq H$ and $V_0\subseteq K$ are finite-dimensional subspaces with orthonormal bases $e_1,\dots,e_p$ and $f_1,\dots,f_q$, then every $z$ in the span of the elementary tensors from $U_0\times V_0$ has a unique expansion $z=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}\,e_a\otimes f_b$ and $\langle z,z\rangle=\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2$; in particular the assignment is an inner product on $H\odot K$; (c) *completion*: the norm completion $(\widehat{H\odot K},\kappa)$ of $H\odot K$ ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]) exists and, with the unique inner product extending the given one, is a complex Hilbert space; $\kappa$ is a linear isometry with dense image, $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$, and any two completions of $H\odot K$ are identified by a unique surjective linear isometry fixing $H\odot K$ pointwise; (d) *product bases*: if $(e_a)_{a\in A}$ and $(f_b)_{b\in B}$ are orthonormal families in $H$ and $K$ whose closed linear spans are $H$ and $K$, then $(\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b))_{(a,b)\in A\times B}$ is an orthonormal family in $\widehat{H\odot K}$ whose closed linear span is $\widehat{H\odot K}$; if $A$ and $B$ are countable then $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is separable. The notation $H\widehat{\otimes}K:=\widehat{H\odot K}$ is used in the rest of this pair. No assertion is made about unbounded operators or algebraic sums of non-completed tensor products.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$ the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or **complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$, $$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$ **Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$, $$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$ **Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is $$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$ which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and $\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$. **The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length. In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of $\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either scalar field.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation $$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$ and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map $$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$ assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore $$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$ which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$. **Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. **Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $P_M$ be the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$. Then: 1. $P_M$ is linear and idempotent, $\operatorname{ran}P_M=M$ and $\ker P_M=M^\perp$; 2. $\langle P_Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,P_My\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$, that is $P_M$ is self-adjoint; 3. $\|P_Mx\|\le\|x\|$ for every $x$, so $P_M$ is a bounded linear operator of norm at most $1$; and if $M\ne\{0\}$, then $\|P_M\|=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map $$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$ is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with $$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$ The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map $$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$ It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness. **The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$, $$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$ so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$ The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice principle is used for this assertion. The same number is the least bound of $T$: $$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$ If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives $$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$ When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$, so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is $$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$ The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$. When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put $$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$ the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite ([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes sense for every subset. **$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by [[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies. **$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries $[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$ onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same cardinality. **Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set $$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$ the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$, $$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$ **$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is *not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove. **Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.** - $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved. - $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$ then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$. - $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$ ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]). - $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$. - $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the above.

Let $m \ge 1$ and write $m = \sigma(M)$, so $M = m-1$. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ $$\big\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n+m-1}{\,m-1\,} = \binom{n+M}{M},$$ and the map $k \mapsto \big\{\, \big(\sum_{j<\sigma(i)} k_j\big) + i \ :\ i < M \,\big\}$ is a bijection of $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$ onto the set of $M$-element subsets of $n+M$. Moreover, for $m \ge 1$ **and $n \ge 1$**, $$\big\lvert\mathcal{C}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n-1}{\,m-1\,}.$$ **The hypothesis $m \ge 1$ is not decoration.** At $m = 0$ the expression $\binom{n+m-1}{m-1}$ would require the value $m-1$ at $m = 0$, and [[def-composition-of-a-natural-number]] records the true counts there: $\lvert\mathcal{W}(0,0)\rvert = 1$ and $\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,0)\rvert = 0$ for $n \ge 1$. The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ in the second display is equally load bearing: at $n = 0$, $m = 1$ the formula would give $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ while $\mathcal{C}(0,1) = \varnothing$.

Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$. Then, in $\mathbb{N}$, $$\binom{n}{k}\cdot k!\cdot (n-k)! = n! ,$$ and consequently: 1. $\binom{n}{k}\cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$ ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]); 2. **integrality**: in $\mathbb{R}$, $\iota\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{\iota(n!)}{\iota(k!)\,\iota((n-k)!)}$, so the familiar quotient $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$ is the canonical natural of a natural number, namely of the count $\binom{n}{k}$; 3. **symmetry**: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$. Here $\iota$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]] and $n-k$ the truncated difference, which for $k \le n$ is the ordinary one.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put $$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$ Then the following four assertions are equivalent: 1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$; 2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$; 3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$ for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]); 4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$. Assertion 2 is the statement $\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,vangle}$. The definitions below do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]). **Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when $$\langle e_i,e_jangle=\delta_{ij}:= egin{cases}1,&i=j,\0,&i

e j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_jangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,tangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,tangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigrangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_jangle=c_j ,$$ so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to $c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$. **Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$ finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the **closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$ containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A **Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal family in $H$. **The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one. **Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$, ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page. **Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the scalars $\langle x,e_iangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map $$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$ is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with $$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$ The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map $$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$ It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness. **The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$, $$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$ so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

derivations.claim: [Product basis] We show by induction on $n$ that $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H^{\otimes n}$. For $n=1$ this is the hypothesis. If it holds for $n$, then by [F1] applied to the orthonormal basis $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ of $H^{\otimes n}$ and $(e_j)_{j\in\{1,\dots,d\}}$ of $H$, the products $e_i\otimes e_j$ form an orthonormal family with dense span in $H^{\otimes(n+1)}=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$; this is the displayed family for $n+1$, and its span is $H^{\otimes(n+1)}$ because $H^{\otimes(n+1)}$ is finite dimensional, so a dense subspace is the whole space. Hence the family is an orthonormal basis, its cardinality is $d\cdot d^n=d^{n+1}$ and $\dim H^{\otimes n}=d^n$, which is (a). [F1, algebra, induction]

[The alternating projection on basis vectors] Let $i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n$. By the action formula of [F2], $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)e_{i_{\pi^{-1}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_{\pi^{-1}(n)}}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\tau\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)e_{i_{\tau(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_{\tau(n)}}$ after the substitution $\tau=\pi^{-1}$. If two entries of $i$ coincide, say $i_k=i_l$ with $k\ne l$, then the transposition $\upsilon=(kl)$ satisfies $e_{i_{\upsilon\tau(1)}}\otimes\cdots=e_{i_{\tau(1)}}\otimes\cdots$ for every $\tau$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\upsilon\tau)=-\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, so the sum pairs to zero and $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ by [F2]. If the entries are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_n\}$ and $i_k=j_{\rho_i(k)}$, then $e_{i_{\tau(1)}}\otimes\cdots=e_{j_{\rho_i\tau(1)}}\otimes\cdots$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i\tau)$; substituting $\omega=\rho_i\tau$ gives $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)}{n!}\sum_{\omega\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\omega)e_{j_{\omega(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\omega(n)}}=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$, which is the second formula of (b). [F2, algebra]

[Orthonormality of the Slater family] For subsets $J,K$ with $|J|=|K|=n$ put $A_{ab}:=\langle e_{j_a},e_{k_b}\rangle=\delta_{j_a,k_b}$. By [F1], $\langle e_J^\wedge,e_K^\wedge\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma,\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{l=1}^n A_{\sigma(l),\pi(l)}$. For each fixed $\pi$ substitute $\sigma=\omega\pi$ and reindex the product by $t=\pi(l)$. Then $\prod_l A_{\sigma(l),\pi(l)}=\prod_t A_{\omega(t),t}$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\omega)$, so the sum over $\pi$ contributes $n!$ and the remaining sum is $\det(A)$ by [F3]. For $J=K$, $A=I_n$ and this is $1$; for $J\ne K$, some $j_a$ is absent from $K$, giving a zero row and determinant $0$. Thus the Slater family is orthonormal. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

[Occupation operators] For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the formula of (d) defines a linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $H^{\otimes n}$; by [F6] applied to the complete orthonormal family $(e_i)$ we have $x=\sum_i\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ and $N_jx=\sum_i|i|_j\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ for every $x$. Self-adjointness: for $x,y\in H^{\otimes n}$ the expansions give $\langle N_jx,y\rangle=\sum_i|i|_j\langle x,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle y,e_i\rangle}=\langle x,N_jy\rangle$ because the numbers $|i|_j$ are real, so $N_j$ is self-adjoint by [F7]; it is bounded because its range is spanned by the finitely many $e_i$ with eigenvalue at most $n$, and $\|N_jx\|\le n\|x\|$. The same computation on the basis vectors $e_i$, on which $N_j$ is diagonal with the real eigenvalues $|i|_j$, gives $N_jN_ke_i=|i|_k|i|_je_i=N_kN_je_i$ and $\sum_jN_je_i=\bigl(\sum_j|i|_j\bigr)e_i=ne_i$; since the $e_i$ form a basis by step 1.1 and both sides of each identity are linear, $N_jN_k=N_kN_j$ and $\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$. This proves the operator statements of (d) except the two eigenvector formulas. [F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

[Slater basis and its dimension] By step 1.2 each $e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$, and each $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)$ is either zero or a multiple of some $e_J^\wedge$; since the $e_i$ form a basis of $H^{\otimes n}$ by step 1.1 and $P_-^{(n)}$ is linear, the closed linear span of $(e_J^\wedge)$ is exactly $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ (a finite-dimensional, hence closed, subspace). By step 1.3 the family is orthonormal, so it is an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$, indexed by the $n$-element subsets $J$ of $\{1,\dots,d\}$; by [F4] there are $\binom dn$ of them, so $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$. e\varnothing$ and $m_\lambda=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)}e_c$ is a nonempty sum of orthonormal vectors of $H^{\otimes n}$, hence nonzero, with $\|m_\lambda\|^2=|\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)|$ by the orthonormality of the product basis in step 1.1 [F1]. If $\lambda
e\mu$ then a word has a unique multiplicity vector, so $\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)\cap\operatorname{orb}(\mu)=\varnothing$ and the inner product of $m_\lambda$ and $m_\mu$ is the empty sum $0$. For $\pi\in S_n$ the map $c\mapsto\pi\cdot c$, $(\pi\cdot c)_k:=c_{\pi^{-1}(k)}$, permutes $\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)$ and $U_\pi e_c=e_{\pi\cdot c}$ by [F2], so $U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$. Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing linear in the first argument ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]). Write $H\odot K$ for the complex vector space of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] applied to $R=\mathbb C$ and the $\mathbb C$-modules $H,K$: its underlying abelian group is the quotient $F/H_0$ of that definition, the class of $e_{(u,v)}$ is written $u\otimes v$, every element of $H\odot K$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $u\otimes v$, and the defining relations make $(u,v)\mapsto u\otimes v$ $\mathbb C$-bilinear. Define, for finite sums, $$\Bigl\langle\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i,\ \sum_j u'_j\otimes v'_j\Bigr\rangle:=\sum_{i,j}\langle u_i,u'_j\rangle_H\,\langle v_i,v'_j\rangle_K .$$ Then: (a) *well-definedness and sesquilinearity*: the displayed value is independent of the representatives of its two arguments and defines a Hermitian sesquilinear form on $H\odot K$, linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; (b) *positive definiteness and orthonormal coordinates*: $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ for every $z\in H\odot K$, with $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ exactly for $z=0$; more precisely, if $U_0\subseteq H$ and $V_0\subseteq K$ are finite-dimensional subspaces with orthonormal bases $e_1,\dots,e_p$ and $f_1,\dots,f_q$, then every $z$ in the span of the elementary tensors from $U_0\times V_0$ has a unique expansion $z=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}\,e_a\otimes f_b$ and $\langle z,z\rangle=\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}|^2$; in particular the assignment is an inner product on $H\odot K$; (c) *completion*: the norm completion $(\widehat{H\odot K},\kappa)$ of $H\odot K$ ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]) exists and, with the unique inner product extending the given one, is a complex Hilbert space; $\kappa$ is a linear isometry with dense image, $\|\kappa(u\otimes v)\|=\|u\|\,\|v\|$, and any two completions of $H\odot K$ are identified by a unique surjective linear isometry fixing $H\odot K$ pointwise; (d) *product bases*: if $(e_a)_{a\in A}$ and $(f_b)_{b\in B}$ are orthonormal families in $H$ and $K$ whose closed linear spans are $H$ and $K$, then $(\kappa(e_a\otimes f_b))_{(a,b)\in A\times B}$ is an orthonormal family in $\widehat{H\odot K}$ whose closed linear span is $\widehat{H\odot K}$; if $A$ and $B$ are countable then $\widehat{H\odot K}$ is separable. The notation $H\widehat{\otimes}K:=\widehat{H\odot K}$ is used in the rest of this pair. No assertion is made about unbounded operators or algebraic sums of non-completed tensor products.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product $$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$ represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors. For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $W\subseteq V$ be a normed subspace. If $W$ admits an ordered basis of finite length, including length zero, then $W$ is closed in $V$. This holds in ZF, without a choice axiom; the ambient space need not be complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), let $H\widehat\otimes H$ be its completed tensor square with inclusion $\kappa$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), and for $n=2$ let $(U_\pi)_{\pi\in S_2}$ and the projections $P_\pm^{(2)}$ be those of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Write $\tau:=U_{(12)}$ for the **exchange operator**, so that $\tau\bigl(\kappa(u\otimes v)\bigr)=\kappa(v\otimes u)$ for $u,v\in H$; in the sequel the inclusion is suppressed and $u\otimes v$ denotes $\kappa(u\otimes v)$. Then: (a) $\tau$ is self-adjoint and $\tau^2=I$; consequently $\tau$ is an isometry with $\tau^{-1}=\tau=\tau^{*}$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); (b) $P_+^{(2)}=\tfrac12(I+\tau)$ and $P_-^{(2)}=\tfrac12(I-\tau)$, and $$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(2)}=\{x\in H\widehat\otimes H:\tau x=x\},\qquad \operatorname{ran}P_-^{(2)}=\{x\in H\widehat\otimes H:\tau x=-x\};$$ (c) for all $u,v\in H$, $$\|u\otimes v+v\otimes u\|^{2}=2\bigl(\|u\|^{2}\|v\|^{2}+|\langle u,v\rangle|^{2}\bigr), \qquad \|u\otimes v-v\otimes u\|^{2}=2\bigl(\|u\|^{2}\|v\|^{2}-|\langle u,v\rangle|^{2}\bigr);$$ in particular, if $u,v$ are orthonormal, then $s:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(u\otimes v+v\otimes u)$ and $a:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(u\otimes v-v\otimes u)$ are orthonormal, $\tau s=s$ and $\tau a=-a$, and both $\operatorname{ran}P_\pm^{(2)}$ are nonzero; (d) whenever $u,v\in H$ are orthonormal, $\tau\kappa(u\otimes v)\ne\kappa(u\otimes v)$. Consequently, if $H$ contains an orthonormal pair (equivalently, $\dim H\ge2$), both exchange eigenspaces contain nonzero vectors and $\tau\ne I$. If $H=\{0\}$ or $\dim H=1$, then $\tau=I$, $P_+^{(2)}=I$ and $P_-^{(2)}=0$; for $H=\{0\}$ the tensor square and both ranges are zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$. (a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). (b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$. (c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$. (d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$ The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice principle is used for this assertion. The same number is the least bound of $T$: $$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$ If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives $$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$ When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$, so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m,n\in\mathbb N$. The standard finite free modules satisfy $$R^m\otimes_RR^n\cong R^{mn},$$ with the tensor products of standard basis vectors corresponding to the standard basis indexed by $m\times n$. If $F$ is a field and $V,W$ are finite-dimensional $F$-vector spaces, then $$\dim_F(V\otimes_FW)=(\dim_FV)(\dim_FW).$$ Both assertions include a zero rank or zero-dimensional factor.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$ with orthonormal basis $(e_1,\dots,e_d)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Let $H^{\otimes n}$ be the $n$-fold completed tensor power with $H^{\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes1}:=H$ and $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), and let $P_\pm^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$, $n\ge1$, be the permutation projections of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. For a multi-index $i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n$ write $$e_i:=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n},\qquad |i|_j:=\#\{k:i_k=j\}\ (j=1,\dots,d).$$ For $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}$ with $|J|=n$, written $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_n\}$, put $$e_J^\wedge:=\frac1{\sqrt{n!}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, e_{j_{\sigma(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\sigma(n)}},$$ and for $\lambda\in W(n,d):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb N^d:\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ put $\operatorname{orb}(\lambda):=\{c\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n:|c|=\lambda\}$ and $m_\lambda:=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)}e_c$. Then: (a) *product basis*: $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H^{\otimes n}$, and $\dim H^{\otimes n}=d^n$; (b) *Slater basis*: for every $J$ with $|J|=n$ one has $e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ and the family $(e_J^\wedge)_{J\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$; it is therefore an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$, $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$, and $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$ when $n>d$. Moreover for every multi-index $i$ one has $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ when two entries of $i$ coincide, and $$P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\,\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$$ when the entries of $i$ are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J$ and $\rho_i\in S_n$ is the unique permutation with $i_k=j_{\rho_i(k)}$; (c) *symmetric basis*: for every $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ the vector $m_\lambda$ is nonzero, the family $(m_\lambda)_{\lambda\in W(n,d)}$ is orthogonal, $U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$ for every $\pi\in S_n$, and for every multi-index $i$ there is a real number $\gamma_i>0$ with $P_+^{(n)}(e_i)=\gamma_i\,m_{|i|}$; consequently $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is the linear span of $(m_\lambda)$, the family $(m_\lambda)$ is an orthogonal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$; (d) *occupation operators*: for $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the map $$N_j:H^{\otimes n}\to H^{\otimes n},\qquad N_jx:=\sum_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}|i|_j\,\langle x,e_i\rangle\,e_i,$$ is a self-adjoint bounded endomorphism, the $N_j$ commute pairwise, $\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$, and $$N_je_J^\wedge=\mathbf 1_J(j)\,e_J^\wedge,\qquad N_jm_\lambda=\lambda_j\,m_\lambda .$$ Consequently both sectors are invariant under every $N_j$, the joint eigenspaces of $(N_1,\dots,N_d)$ inside $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ are the lines $\mathbb Ce_J^\wedge$ (one for each $n$-element subset $J$, with eigenvalue vector $\mathbf 1_J$), and the joint eigenspaces inside $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ are the lines $\mathbb Cm_\lambda$ (one for each $\lambda\in W(n,d)$, with eigenvalue vector $\lambda$).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation $$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$ and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map $$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$ assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore $$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$ which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$. **Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. **Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

derivations.claim: [Identification] By [F1] the inclusion $\kappa:H\odot V\to H\widehat\otimes V$ is a linear isometry with dense image; if $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ are orthonormal bases of $H$ and $V$, then the $mk$ elements $e_a\otimes f_b$ span the algebraic tensor product by bilinearity, so $\kappa[H\odot V]$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space $H\widehat\otimes V$, hence closed by [F3], and a dense closed subspace is the whole space; thus $\kappa$ is onto and identifies the two spaces, and the same argument applies to the algebraic and completed tensor products of $H\otimes V$ with itself and of $H\otimes H$ with $V\otimes V$, whose algebraic parts are spanned by finitely many elementary tensors. This proves (a). [F1, F3, algebra]

[The regrouping map and its inverse] Define $\Phi(u,v,\chi,\chi'):=(u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')$ for $u,v\in H$, $\chi,\chi'\in V$; it is multilinear in its four arguments, so by [F2] it corresponds to a unique linear map on the four-fold algebraic tensor product and, by the parenthesization independence of [F2] together with the identification of step 1.1, to a unique linear map $\Theta$ on $(H\otimes V)\widehat\otimes(H\otimes V)$ with the displayed values on elementary tensors; uniqueness holds because those elementary tensors span the space. Likewise $\Psi\bigl((u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')\bigr):=(u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')$ is multilinear and defines a linear map $\Psi$ on $(H\otimes H)\widehat\otimes(V\otimes V)$. On elementary tensors $\Psi\Theta=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Theta\Psi=\mathrm{id}$, and two linear maps agreeing on a spanning set agree everywhere; hence $\Theta$ is a linear isomorphism with inverse $\Psi$, which is the existence and inverse statement of (b). [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

[Unitarity] For elementary tensors $x=(u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')$ and $y=(u'\otimes\chi'')\otimes(v'\otimes\chi''')$ in the domain the inner-product identities of [F1] give $\langle\Theta x,\Theta y\rangle=\langle u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'\rangle\langle\chi\otimes\chi',\chi''\otimes\chi'''\rangle=\langle u,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle\langle\chi,\chi''\rangle\langle\chi',\chi'''\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$; the difference of the two sesquilinear forms vanishes on all pairs of elementary tensors, and since every vector is a finite sum of elementary tensors by [F1] it vanishes identically, so $\Theta$ is an isometry; being invertible by step 2.1 it is unitary, which completes (b). [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

[Intertwining with the exchange operators] For $u,v\in H$, $\chi,\chi'\in V$ one computes with [F4] and [F5] that $\Theta\tau_{H\otimes V}\bigl((u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')\bigr)=\Theta\bigl((v\otimes\chi')\otimes(u\otimes\chi)\bigr)=(v\otimes u)\otimes(\chi'\otimes\chi)$ and $(\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)\Theta\bigl((u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')\bigr)=(\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)\bigl((u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')\bigr)=(v\otimes u)\otimes(\chi'\otimes\chi)$; both sides are bounded linear maps agreeing on the spanning set of elementary tensors, so they agree everywhere, which is (c). [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

[Symmetriser identities] By [F4], $P_\pm^{(H\otimes V)}=\frac12(I\pm\tau_{H\otimes V})$, $P_\pm^{(H)}=\frac12(I\pm\tau_H)$ and $P_\pm^{(V)}=\frac12(I\pm\tau_V)$; using step 3.2 to move $\Theta$ past $\tau_{H\otimes V}$ and the linearity and multiplicativity of the tensor product of operators [F5], one obtains on the whole space $\Theta P_-^{(H\otimes V)}=\frac12\Theta-\frac12(\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)\Theta=\bigl(\frac12-\frac12\tau_H\otimes\tau_V\bigr)\Theta=\bigl(P_-^{(H)}\otimes P_+^{(V)}+P_+^{(H)}\otimes P_-^{(V)}\bigr)\Theta$, because $\frac12(I-\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)=\frac12(I-\tau_H)\otimes\frac12(I+\tau_V)+\frac12(I+\tau_H)\otimes\frac12(I-\tau_V)$ and its sign-reversed analogue are identities of bounded operators; this proves the first assertion of (d), and the computation with both signs reversed gives the second. [F4, F5, step 3.2, algebra]

[Direct-sum decompositions] By [F7] the operators $P_-^{(H)}\otimes P_+^{(V)}$ and $P_+^{(H)}\otimes P_-^{(V)}$ are orthogonal projections whose product is $(P_-^{(H)}P_+^{(H)})\otimes(P_+^{(V)}P_-^{(V)})=0$, so their sum is an orthogonal projection with range the orthogonal direct sum of the two ranges; by step 4.1 and the unitarity of step 3.1, the image of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(H\otimes V)}$ under $\Theta$ is that direct sum, and the same argument with the second identity of step 4.1 gives the symmetric-sector decomposition, completing (d). [F7, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

[Vector identities] Applying the first identity of step 4.1 to the elementary tensor $(u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')$ and using the linearity of $\Theta$ and of tensor products of operators gives $\Theta P_-^{(H\otimes V)}\bigl((u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')\bigr)=\bigl(P_-^{(H)}\otimes P_+^{(V)}+P_+^{(H)}\otimes P_-^{(V)}\bigr)\bigl((u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')\bigr)=P_+^{(H)}(u\otimes v)\otimes P_-^{(V)}(\chi\otimes\chi')+P_-^{(H)}(u\otimes v)\otimes P_+^{(V)}(\chi\otimes\chi')$, which is the first identity of (e); the second follows in the same way from the second identity of step 4.1. [step 4.1, algebra]

[Dimensions] By step 5.1 and the unitarity of step 3.1, $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(H\otimes V)}=\dim(\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(H)}\otimes\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(V)})+\dim(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(H)}\otimes\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(V)})$; by [F6] applied to the $m$- and $k$-dimensional spaces this is $\binom m2\binom{k+1}2+\binom{m+1}2\binom k2$, which are the displayed summand dimensions, and expanding the two products gives $\frac{m(m-1)k(k+1)+m(m+1)k(k-1)}4=\frac{mk(mk-1)}2=\binom{mk}2$, which is (f). [F6, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra]

[Assembly] Step 1.1 proves (a), steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove (b), step 3.2 proves (c), steps 4.1 and 5.1 prove (d), step 5.2 proves (e) and step 6.1 proves (f). Only the cited linear algebra, tensor products and permutation projections were used, under the Countable Choice hypotheses of [F1], [F2] and [F5]; no physical reading of the factors is asserted. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 6.1] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 2.1 construct $\Theta$ and check its unitarity on spanned sets, so the zero vector and the empty sum are covered; the dimensions of clause (f) are computed for arbitrary $m,k\ge1$.
Step 2.1 evaluates the isometry on the zero vector by sesquilinearity, and step 3.1 treats the zero operator identity at the zero vector.

boundaries.reason: No unit-sized parameter is distinguished; $m$ and $k$ are arbitrary positive dimensions.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 3.2 and 5.1 cover $m=1$ or $k=1$, where one of the summands has dimension zero by the boundary values of the binomial coefficient, and step 4.1 treats the sum of two projections one of which may vanish.

boundaries.reason: No interval or limiting parameter occurs; all objects are finite-dimensional and algebraic.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared and used through [F1] and [F5] in steps 1.1 and 2.1 for the tensor constructions and the bounded tensor maps.
Step 2.1 proves that the displayed elementary assignment determines $\Theta$ uniquely and that $\Theta$ is invertible, the forward half of the regrouping statement.
Step 2.1 exhibits the inverse $\Psi$ with the reverse assignment, the converse half of the regrouping statement.

citations.quote: **(a) Adopted readings.** Adopt the state and composition postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1) and the identical-particle and spin postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] (P6), read with the state space vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]] and the quantities and units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the choice hypothesis of the cited tensor construction. **(b) Declared species and sector.** A **declared species sector** of the model consists of: a nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $H$, the **one-particle space** of the species, as assigned in P1; a mass parameter $m>0$ in kg; a spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and the internal factor $V_{s}=\mathbb C^{2s+1}$ of P6 clause (ii), with the **orbital factor** $H_{\mathrm{sp}}$ the factor carrying no internal degree of freedom when the one-particle space is given as a completed product $H_{\mathrm{sp}}\widehat\otimes V_{s}$; for the massive spin-$s$ model of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] the one-particle space is $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{2s+1})$, whose spin components are the internal factor of P6 clause (ii) in the reading of that definition; a **statistics choice** $\sigma\in\{+,-\}$, where $+$ declares the species **bosonic** and $-$ declares it **fermionic**; and, for a charged species, a charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs. The parameters and the statistics choice are empirical model assignments with their uncertainties, in the sense of P6 clause (iii); no value and no statistics choice is derived by this definition. **(c) The $n$-particle sector.** Fix $n\ge1$. The **labelled $n$-particle space** of the species is the $n$-fold completed tensor power $H^{\otimes n}$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), whose tensor factors are mathematical labels and not observable particle identities, equipped with the permutation unitaries $(U_\pi)_{\pi\in S_n}$ and the sector projections $P_\sigma^{(n)}$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]), where $P_+^{(n)}$ is the symmetrizing projection and $P_-^{(n)}$ the alternating projection. The **$n$-particle sector space** of the declared species is $$\mathfrak H_n^\sigma:=\operatorname{ran}P_\sigma^{(n)}\ \subseteq\ H^{\otimes n},$$ a closed linear subspace carrying the inner product of $H^{\otimes n}$; on it every permutation acts by the scalar $$U_\pi|_{\mathfrak H_n^\sigma}=\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)\, \mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak H_n^\sigma},\qquad \operatorname{sgn}_+(\pi)=1,\quad \operatorname{sgn}_-(\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi),$$ by clause (c) of the cited permutation lemma. For $n=1$ one has $\mathfrak H_1^+=\mathfrak H_1^-=H$. **(d) Declared sector preparations.** A **declared sector preparation** of $n$ particles of the species is a state of the framework on the sector space, that is a density operator $$\rho\in D(\mathfrak H_n^\sigma)$$ in the sense of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] and clause (a) of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], read as the state assigned to the preparation by P1 clause (iii). A **pure sector preparation** is a pure state, i.e. the rank-one operator of a unit ray of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$; a statistical mixture of sector preparations is a convex combination. The sector is part of the declaration of the species: a model that declares one statistics choice does not switch it within the same declaration. **(e) Sector quantities.** Let $A$ be a linear operator on the labelled space $H^{\otimes n}$ with domain $D(A)$. The model reads $A$ as a **quantity of the declared sector** only when $A$ **preserves the sector**, $$P_\sigma^{(n)}D(A)\subseteq D(A),\qquad A\,\mathfrak H_n^\sigma\subseteq \mathfrak H_n^\sigma,$$ in which case the **sector restriction** $A_\sigma:=A|_{\mathfrak H_n^\sigma}$ with domain $D(A)\cap\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ is part of the declaration and is the quantity actually read on sector preparations; a bounded quantity preserves the sector exactly when it commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$. An operator that does not preserve the sector is not read on the sector; in particular no quantity of a single labelled factor is assumed to define a quantity of the sector unless it preserves it. If $A_\sigma$ is self-adjoint, its outcome law in a sector preparation is the law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] read on $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$. **(f) Status and scope.** Clauses (a)-(e) fix the vocabulary with which the framework reads the adopted P6 assumptions: they add no assumption to P1 and P6, and the permutation invariance of sector preparations and of sector readouts is a conditional consequence proved on this page ([[pthm-nrqm-identical-particles-permutation-invariance]]), not a content of this definition. The definition asserts no spin-statistics theorem, no dynamics, no measurement instrument and no empirical fact; whether a laboratory ensemble is described by a declared sector preparation is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7, not a consequence of the declaration.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor. (a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with $$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. (b) The operators $$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$ (with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections. (c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$. (d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$. Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition. **(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment $$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$ the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b). **(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$, and an exact value of a quantity with no eigenvalues is an idealization outside the assignment, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2. **(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable. **(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation. **(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it. **(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about sharp and unsharp real-valued quantities. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The latter is the explicit hypothesis used to obtain the spectral PVM of a general self-adjoint operator from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] in clause (ii); consumers invoking this construction inherit it. **(i) Sharp observables.** An **ideal sharp real-valued quantity** (observable) of a system with state space $H$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), together with a declared unit in which its real spectral coordinate is read; the unit is part of the assignment, and no numerical value of the coordinate is asserted by the assignment. Symmetry of $A$ on a small domain is not sufficient for self-adjointness, and the domain is a declared part of the observable. **(ii) Spectral probability.** Let $E_{A}$ be the spectral projection-valued measure of the self-adjoint operator $A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the **probability of the outcome in $B$** is $$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{A}(B)\bigr),\qquad\text{and for a pure preparation }[\psi]\text{ it is }\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}.$$ By clause (b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] the assignment $B\mapsto\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets ([[def-probability-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). It is the general form of the Born rule adopted here. **(iii) Nature of the outcome law.** The probability law is a measure, not necessarily a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and not necessarily a finite or countable sum of point masses: a self-adjoint operator with continuous spectrum ordinarily has no normalizable eigenvector at a point of its continuous spectrum, so an "exact value" of a continuum quantity is not represented by a normalized state. An ideal point value is an idealization; a real detector reports a finite-resolution outcome, that is, the probability of a declared Borel set $B$ such as a bin, and the recorded-event probability is that of (ii) for the bin, not the value of a density at a point. **(iv) Unsharp finite outcomes.** Outcomes of a finite-resolution apparatus with finitely many channels are described, when the idealization uses bounded effects, by a finite family $(F_{a})_{a=1}^{p}$ of bounded operators with $0\le F_{a}\le I$ in the quadratic-form order and $\sum_{a}F_{a}=I$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]] clause (a)), the **outcome probabilities** being $p_{a}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})\ge0$, $\sum_{a}p_{a}=1$ by clause (b) of the same lemma. This unsharp extension is an operational description tied to an apparatus model; it is not obtained from the sharp observable by mathematical manipulation alone, and the effects alone do not determine what happens to the state after the outcome (P3). **(v) Moments are a separate matter.** Statements about the mean, variance or higher moments of the outcome law require the corresponding integrability of $t\mapsto t^{n}$ against $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ and are not part of this postulate; where they are used they are stated with their hypotheses. In particular the existence of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for an unbounded $A$ is not asserted. **(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model. They assert nothing about which quantities of a concrete apparatus are sharp, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome or about the completeness of the description; a laboratory record is a classical event whose relation to the model is a tested identification with uncertainty, in the sense of P7.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-inner-product-space]]) and let $U:H\to K$ be a bijective linear map with $$\langle Ux,Uy\rangle_K=\langle x,y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H .$$ Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_T$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), and define $$D(T'):=U D(T),\qquad T'(Ux):=U(Tx)\quad(x\in D(T)).$$ Then: (a) $T'$ is well defined, linear, densely defined and self-adjoint on $K$; (b) the assignment $E(B):=U E_T(B) U^{-1}$ on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular projection-valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, and it is the spectral projection-valued measure of $T'$; (c) for every unit vector $x\in H$ the scalar laws of the two operators agree, $$\mu^{T'}_{Ux}(B):=\|E(B)Ux\|_K^2=\|E_T(B)x\|_H^2=:\mu^{T}_x(B)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel});$$ (d) $\sigma(T')=\sigma(T)$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]). **The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.** [[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and $$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$ If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and $BA$ are trace class and $$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

**Density operators.** Let $H
e\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $ho$ with $\operatorname{tr}ho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted $$D(H):=\{ho:ho\ 	ext{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$ An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here. **Pure states.** A state $ho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with $$ho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,uangle u\quad(x\in H),$$ where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map $$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{
u(\psi),
u(\psi)},$$ on the ray space $R(H)$, with $
u$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is $$\widehatho(\psi):= rac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}= rac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$ which equals $T_{
u(\psi),

The **purity** of $ho$ is the real number $$\mathcal P(ho):=\operatorname{tr}(ho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$ The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only. **Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

derivations.claim: [Invariance] Let $x,y\in\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$. By [F1] one has $U_\pi^{*}x=\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)^{-1}x=\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)x$ and likewise for $y$, so $\langle U_\pi\rho U_\pi^{*}x,y\rangle=\langle\rho U_\pi^{*}x,U_\pi^{*}y\rangle=\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)^{2}\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle\rho x,y\rangle$ by the unitarity of $U_\pi$ and the sesquilinearity of the inner product. Since $x,y$ are arbitrary, $U_\pi\rho U_\pi^{*}=\rho$; multiplying this identity on the left by $U_\pi^{*}$ and on the right by $U_\pi$ and using $U_\pi^{*}U_\pi=I$ gives $U_\pi^{*}\rho U_\pi=\rho$ as well. This proves (a). [F1, F5, algebra]

[Sector-preserving case] If $A$ preserves the sector and $U_\pi AU_\pi^{*}=A$ on its domain for every $\pi$, then $A_\pi=A$ and clause (b) is vacuous for such $A$; the sector restriction of clause (e) of the sector definition is the quantity read on sector preparations, and its law agrees with the law of $A$ by [F2]. This is (c). [F1, F2, algebra]

[Relabelled laws] Fix $\pi$ and an assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$. Since $U_\pi$ is a bijective linear isometry of $H^{\otimes n}$ and $A$ is self-adjoint, [F3] gives that $A_\pi=U_\pi AU_\pi^{*}$ is self-adjoint on the domain $U_\pi D(A)$ with spectral measure $E_{A_\pi}(B)=U_\pi E_A(B)U_\pi^{*}$. Hence for every preparation $\rho$ and Borel $B$, $\mu^{A_\pi}_\rho(B)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho U_\pi E_A(B)U_\pi^{*})$ by [F2]. Because $\rho$ is trace class and $U_\pi E_A(B)$ is bounded, [F4] applied twice gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho U_\pi E_A(B)U_\pi^{*})=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^{*}\rho U_\pi E_A(B))$; by step 1.1 the middle factor is $\rho$, so $\mu^{A_\pi}_\rho(B)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(B))=\mu^{A}_\rho(B)$, which is (b) in the general form; for bounded $A$ the same computation with $A$ in place of $E_A(B)$ gives the displayed trace identity. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

[Assembly and scope] Step 1.1 proves (a), step 2.1 proves (b) and step 1.2 proves (c). The proof uses only the adopted sector of P6, the readings of P1 and P2, and the cited spectral and trace mathematics under the declared choice hypotheses; no measured invariance, no dynamics and no species assignment is asserted. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎
